sections.skill: Build a credit history with low utilization, on-time payments, and starter credit products

questions.prompt: Tia's card has a $1,500 limit, and her statement balance is $450. What is her credit utilization?
questions.intro: Credit utilization = card balances ÷ credit limits × 100. It is a major part of the "amounts owed" score factor. Lower utilization generally helps scores; a common guideline is to stay below about 30%, and lower is better.
sources: myFICO (Fair Isaac Corporation): FICO score factor weights: payment history 35%, amounts owed 30%, length of credit history 15%, new credit 10%, credit mix 10%; scores range 300-850. (https://www.myfico.com/credit-education/whats-in-your-credit-score)

AnnualCreditReport.com (authorized by federal law) / FTC: Consumers can get free credit reports from Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion; free weekly reports have been made permanent. (https://www.annualcreditreport.com)

CFPB (Credit card grace period): A grace period, if the card offers one, lets you avoid interest on new purchases by paying the full statement balance by the due date; it usually does not apply to cash advances. (https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-grace-period-for-a-credit-card-en-47/)

questions.prompt: Max has two cards: $300 balance on a $1,000 limit and $700 on a $2,500 limit. What is his overall utilization (nearest tenth)?
questions.intro: Overall utilization adds all balances and divides by all limits.

misconceptions.C: Divides by the larger limit only

sources: myFICO (Fair Isaac Corporation): FICO score factor weights: payment history 35%, amounts owed 30%, length of credit history 15%, new credit 10%, credit mix 10%; scores range 300-850. (https://www.myfico.com/credit-education/whats-in-your-credit-score)

questions.prompt: Leo has no credit history. Which product is designed to help someone start building credit?

choices.text: A secured credit card backed by a cash deposit
A savings account that comes with no card attached

questions.correct_answer: A secured credit card backed by a cash deposit
questions.intro: Starter options include a secured credit card (you put down a deposit that usually becomes your limit), a credit-builder loan (payments are saved for you and released at the end), and being added as an authorized user on a parent's card. Paying on time builds history.
questions.feedback: A secured card reports like a regular card but is backed by a deposit.

misconceptions.B: Usually not reported and very costly

questions.prompt: Leo is added as an authorized user on his mother's card. Her account has a long on-time history and low utilization. What can this do?

choices.text: Make Leo responsible for her past debts
Give Leo his own separate credit limit and account
Help Leo's credit file show positive history

questions.correct_answer: Help Leo's credit file show positive history
questions.intro: An authorized user can use someone else's card. Many issuers report the account to the authorized user's credit file too, which can help, or hurt if the account is misused.
questions.feedback: The account's positive history may appear on Leo's report.

questions.prompt: Which plan builds credit with the LEAST cost?

choices.text: Carry a balance each month to show activity
Max out the card, then pay the minimum
Never use the card at all
Charge a small bill and pay it in full

questions.correct_answer: Charge a small bill and pay it in full
questions.feedback: Small, regular purchases paid in full on time build history without purchase interest on a card with a grace period.

questions.feedback: A larger denominator lowers the percent.

sections.skill: Credit-builder loans and secured cards in detail

questions.prompt: A credit-builder loan of $600 is held in a savings account while Ana makes 12 payments of $52. What does she receive at the end, and what did it cost?
questions.intro: With a credit-builder loan, the lender holds the loan amount in an account while you make payments. Payments are reported to bureaus, and you receive the money at the end. The cost is the interest and fees.

questions.prompt: Leo opens a secured card with a $300 deposit and a $300 limit. Each month his statement reports a $30 balance, and he has no other cards. What utilization is reported each month?
questions.intro: A secured card works like a regular credit card for utilization: the balance reported to the credit bureaus (usually the statement balance) ÷ the credit limit.

misconceptions.C: Uses the deposit as a percent

questions.prompt: After a year of on-time payments, some issuers "graduate" a secured card. What usually happens?

choices.text: The deposit is kept as a fee
It becomes a regular card; the deposit is returned
The card is closed and a penalty is charged to Leo
Leo must pay a new deposit

questions.correct_answer: It becomes a regular card; the deposit is returned
questions.intro: Many secured cards review accounts after a period of good use and may convert them to regular (unsecured) cards.
questions.feedback: Graduation returns the deposit and keeps the account history.

questions.prompt: Which question should Leo ask before opening a secured card?

choices.text: Does the issuer report to all three credit bureaus?
Does the card offer cash-back rewards on purchases?
Will the deposit earn interest like savings?
Will it let me skip payments?

questions.correct_answer: Does the issuer report to all three credit bureaus?
questions.intro: A secured card helps build credit only if the issuer reports your payments to the credit bureaus.
questions.feedback: Reporting to the bureaus is what builds credit.

misconceptions.B: Focuses on rewards instead of credit building
misconceptions.C: Confuses a secured card deposit with savings

questions.prompt: A secured card has a $49 annual fee and 25.99% APR; another has a $0 fee and 28.99% APR. Both have a grace period on purchases. Leo will use it only for purchases and pay in full on time every month. Which is cheaper?

choices.text: The $49-fee card, because its APR is lower

questions.intro: When you keep a purchase grace period by paying the full balance on time every month, the APR does not affect your cost, but annual fees do.
questions.feedback: Paying in full means no purchase interest, so the annual fee is the only cost.

misconceptions.A: APR does not matter if paid in full

questions.prompt: Which step comes FIRST in a safe credit-building plan for a student?

choices.text: Apply for five cards at once
Spend up to the limit each month to show activity
Set up autopay for the full statement balance

questions.correct_answer: Set up autopay for the full statement balance
questions.intro: The key habits for building credit are on-time payment, low balances, and few new applications.
questions.feedback: Autopay for the full balance, with enough money in checking, greatly lowers the risk of late payments and purchase interest from day one.

questions.feedback: A 30-day late payment is reported and can hurt a score for years.

choices.text: A hard inquiry that lowers her score for years
A shorter average age of accounts

misconceptions.D: Confuses a limit increase with opening a new account

choices.text: Check free reports and scores regularly
Apply for new cards to see if she is approved
Apply for loans now and then to see if approved

questions.correct_answer: Check free reports and scores regularly

questions.feedback: Free reports and scores show progress without cost or inquiries.
